title: Fire, Even Covered, Can Be Known
story:
"Enjoy ye all," Kunti called from the inner room, without looking out. The five brothers had come home to the potter's house in the evening and told their mother they had brought alms that day; and Kunti, who had not yet seen her sons, answered as the mother of Brahmanas should. "Enjoy ye all what ye have obtained."

The moment after, she saw Draupadi — and cried out, "Oh, what have I said?"

She had told five sons to enjoy, together, the alms they had brought; and the alms was the daughter of the king of Panchala. Anxious from fear of sin, Kunti took the cheerful princess by the hand and went to Yudhishthira. "The daughter of king Yajnasena was represented to me by thy younger brothers as the alms they had obtained," she said, "and from ignorance, O king, I said, 'Enjoy ye all what hath been obtained.' Tell me, O bull of the Kuru race, how my speech may not become untrue, how sin may not touch the daughter of the king of Panchala, and how she may not become uneasy."

Yudhishthira reflected for a moment and consoled his mother; then he turned to Arjuna. "By thee, O Phalguna, hath Yajnasena's daughter been won. It is proper, therefore, that thou shouldst wed her. Igniting the sacred fire, take thou her hand with due rites."

But Arjuna shook his head. "O king, do not make me a participator in sin. Thy behest is not conformable to virtue; that is the path followed by the sinful. Thou shouldst wed first, then the strong-armed Bhima, then myself, then Nakula, and last of all Sahadeva. All of us are obedient to thee; command us as thou likest."

The brothers looked at one another, and at Draupadi; and the beauty of Panchali, fashioned by the Creator himself, entered their hearts, and the god of desire pressed upon their senses. Yudhishthira, watching his younger brothers, understood what was passing in their minds, and remembered the words of the sage Krishna-Dwaipayana. From fear of a division amongst the brothers, he spoke: "The auspicious Draupadi shall be the common wife of us all."

It was then that two more visitors came to the potter's house. Krishna, suspecting that the five men he had seen at the svayamvara were none other than the heroes of the Kuru race, had come with Balarama; and entering, they beheld Yudhishthira of the well-developed long arms seated there, and his younger brothers passing the splendour of fire sitting around him. Vasudeva approached the foremost of virtuous men, touched the feet of the son of Kunti, and said, "I am Krishna." And Balarama did the same. The Pandavas, beholding Krishna and Balarama, expressed great delight; and the two heroes of the Yadu race touched also the feet of Kunti, their father's sister.

Then Yudhishthira, gazing at Krishna, asked the question that had been burning in him. "How, O Vasudeva, hast thou been able to trace us, as we are living in disguise?"

Krishna smiled. "Fire, even if it is covered, can be known. Who else among men than the Pandavas could exhibit such might? Ye sons of Pandu, by sheer good fortune have ye escaped from that fierce fire; and by sheer good fortune the wicked son of Dhritarashtra and his counsellors have not succeeded in accomplishing their wishes. Blest be ye, and grow ye in prosperity like a fire in a cave, gradually growing and spreading itself all around. And lest any of the monarchs recognise ye, let us return."

And the two Yadava princes went out again into the evening, as quietly as they had come, leaving the potter's house to keep its secret a little longer.
reflection: Krishna's answer — that fire, even covered, can be known — cuts both ways. The disguise holds not because the brothers are invisible, but because the people who see through it choose to protect the secret instead of revealing it. Recognition and restraint are both acts of friendship, and the visit ends the moment it might betray them.
next_story_tease: In the days that followed, the potter's house prepared for a wedding — and Krishna prepared a gift.
hero_scene: By lamplight in a potter's house, Krishna and Balarama touch the feet of Yudhishthira, who sits among his brothers still dressed in Brahmana robes, while the five disguised princes rise in delight and Kunti looks on; clay pots and the potter's wheel surround them.
